summary: Describes version 3 of the Network Time Protocol, its formal structure, and information useful for implementing it. NTP synchronizes computer clocks across the Internet. This version is historic and was replaced by RFC 5905.

eli5.summary: Computers each keep their own clock, and clocks drift. NTP lets computers ask each other the time and fix their clocks so everyone agrees.

questions: how does network time protocol work
how does ntp calculate clock offset
what is a stratum in ntp
subtitle: Version 3 of the protocol that keeps computer clocks in step across the Internet, with its algorithms and error analysis.

tldr.problem: Computers on a large network each keep their own clock, and these drift apart, so there is a need to synchronize time reliably over paths with variable delay and unreliable networks.
tldr.mechanism: NTP exchanges timestamped UDP messages between servers arranged in strata, computes the clock offset and roundtrip delay from four timestamps, filters and selects the best sources, and then steers the local clock gradually.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1305 is now Historic. It obsoletes RFC 958, RFC 1059 and RFC 1119 and was itself replaced by RFC 5905.

today: RFC 1305 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 5905, and it had itself obsoleted RFC 958, RFC 1059 and RFC 1119.

sections.title: What NTP Version 3 Is
sections.content:
This document is the formal specification of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) Version 3, used to synchronize timekeeping among a set of distributed time servers and clients. It is intended primarily for implementors. NTP was first described in RFC 958, then evolved through Version 1 (RFC 1059) and Version 2 (RFC 1119). It is built on IP and UDP, though it is readily adaptable to other protocol suites.

Version 3 supersedes Version 2 but, as the preface says, neither changes the protocol in any significant way nor obsoletes previous versions or existing implementations. The motivation was to refine the analysis and implementation models for much higher network speeds. It rewrote the local-clock algorithm, added an optional algorithm to combine the offsets of several peers, corrected minor errors, and changed how delay, offset and dispersion are calculated so that errors are bounded.

The ASCII text of this RFC is an approximate rendering of a PostScript original, so most figures and tables are missing from it.
sections.eli5: This is the rulebook for a game where computers agree on what time it is. Version 3 mostly makes the same game smoother and more accurate.

sections.title: Servers, Strata and the Time Hierarchy
sections.content:
In the NTP model, a number of primary reference sources, synchronized by wire or radio to national standards, are attached to widely accessible hosts and run as primary time servers. Secondary servers get time from them over the Internet and pass it on to other hosts. The accuracy of each server is described by its stratum: primary servers are stratum one and each level down is one greater. The subnet is intended to form a hierarchical master-slave configuration that must never form a loop.

Paths are chosen with a variant of the Bellman-Ford routing algorithm that builds minimum-weight spanning trees rooted at the primary servers. The metric is the scaled stratum plus the synchronization distance, which is the dispersion plus one-half the absolute delay. If every primary server fails, distances ratchet upward to a preselected maximum treated as infinity, after which a server drops off the subnet and free-runs on its last determined time and frequency.

NTP produces three products relative to a reference clock: clock offset, roundtrip delay and dispersion, the last being the maximum error of the local clock. There is no peer discovery or virtual-circuit management. Data integrity relies on the IP and UDP checksums, and no flow control or retransmission is provided or necessary.
sections.eli5: A few clocks at the top are checked against the best watches in the world. Each level below copies the level above, and the rules make sure nobody ends up copying their own copy in a circle.

sections.title: Timestamps and the Message Format
sections.content:
An NTP timestamp is a 64-bit unsigned fixed-point number of seconds relative to 0h on 1 January 1900, with the integer part in the first 32 bits and the fraction in the last 32 bits. The precision is about 200 picoseconds. A zero timestamp means the value is invalid or undefined. The field will overflow some time in 2036, so some external means would be needed to tell time relative to 1900 from time relative to 2036, and the RFC mentions a period of 136 years.

An NTP message follows the UDP header and carries the leap indicator, version number (3), mode, stratum, poll interval, precision, root delay, root dispersion, a 32-bit reference clock identifier and four timestamps (reference, originate, receive and transmit). An optional authenticator comes last. For stratum 0 or 1 the identifier is a four-octet ASCII string, and for stratum 2 and above it is the Internet address of the peer used for synchronization. NTP uses UDP port 123.

The leap indicator is a two-bit warning: 00 no warning, 01 the last minute has 61 seconds, 10 the last minute has 59 seconds, and 11 an alarm condition meaning the clock is not synchronized.
sections.eli5: Each message is a note carrying four time stamps, like the times a ball was thrown and caught, plus a few facts about how good the sender's clock is.

sections.title: Modes and Measuring Offset and Delay
sections.content:
An association can run in one of five modes. Symmetric active and symmetric passive peers are willing both to synchronize and to be synchronized by each other. A client is willing to be synchronized by a server but not to synchronize it. A server is created on arrival of a client request, exists only to reply, and needs to keep no state between requests. A broadcast host periodically announces time to all peers on a typically high-speed LAN, which then use a preconfigured latency of a few milliseconds. If both peers use the same mode, other than symmetric active, each ignores the other.

When a reply arrives, the four timestamps are used to calculate delay and offset. With T(i-3) the originate time, T(i-2) the receive time, T(i-1) the transmit time and T(i) the time of arrival, the roundtrip delay is (T(i) - T(i-3)) - (T(i-1) - T(i-2)) and the offset is ((T(i-2) - T(i-3)) + (T(i-1) - T(i))) / 2. The order and timing of messages are unimportant and reliable delivery is not required.
sections.eli5: To find out how far off your watch is, you note when you asked, when the other kid heard you, when they answered, and when you heard back. The gaps tell you both the travel time and your error.

sections.title: Filtering, Selection and the Local Clock
sections.content:
Section 4 describes suggested algorithms that are not an integral part of the NTP specification, since better ones may be devised. The clock-filter procedure keeps a shift register of recent samples per peer and picks the one with the minimum distance. The clock-selection procedure has two parts: an intersection algorithm, adapted from the Digital Time Service, that casts out falsetickers (clocks that do not keep to a trusted standard), and a clustering algorithm that repeatedly casts out outliers until the best survivors remain.

The local-clock section then describes how a host adjusts its logical clock. Small corrections are applied as gradual phase adjustments to avoid discontinuities. When a correction exceeds the maximum aperture, a step change replaces the clock, which is rare and typically happens after a reboot, and the leap bits are set to unsynchronized and the peer filters are cleared. The appendices add an optional clock-combining algorithm, a mathematical clock model and an error analysis.
sections.eli5: The computer asks several helpers, throws away answers that look wrong, trusts the best ones, and then slowly nudges its watch instead of jumping it.

sections.title: Access Control and Authentication
sections.content:
The design intends that accidental or malicious tampering with one time server should not generally cause timekeeping errors elsewhere. This depends on redundant servers and diverse network paths, and on tampering not happening at many servers at the same time.

Access control is not required, but a simple scheme treats associations preconfigured in symmetric or client mode as trusted and all others as friendly. Only trusted accesses can make a peer the synchronization source. A fuller design could use an access-control list of a 32-bit address, a 32-bit mask and a three-bit mode.

Appendix C defines an optional authenticator of 96 bits: a 32-bit key identifier and a 64-bit crypto-checksum, computed with the Data Encryption Standard encryption algorithm, so decryption need not be shipped. It can be enabled per peer. The RFC warns that encryption can be CPU-intensive and can degrade accuracy unless precautions are taken.
sections.eli5: Because many helpers are asked, one liar cannot easily fool a computer. For extra safety, messages can carry a secret signature that only trusted friends know how to make.

viz.caption: NTP MESSAGE FIELDS AND WIDTHS (RFC 1305, APPENDIX A)

fields.name: Poll
fields.desc: Maximum interval between messages, a power of two in seconds.

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: Precision of the local clock, a power of two in seconds.

fields.name: Root Delay
fields.desc: Total roundtrip delay to the primary reference source.

fields.name: Root Dispersion
fields.desc: Maximum error relative to the primary reference source.

fields.name: Reference Timestamp
fields.desc: When the local clock was last set or corrected.

fields.name: Originate Timestamp
fields.desc: When the request left the client.

fields.name: Receive Timestamp
fields.desc: When the request arrived at the server.

fields.name: Transmit Timestamp
fields.desc: When the reply left the server.

items.label: Symmetric active
items.desc: Peer that sends periodic messages and is willing to synchronize and be synchronized.

items.label: Symmetric passive
items.desc: Created on arrival of a symmetric active message.

items.label: Client
items.desc: Asks to be synchronized, but does not synchronize the peer.

items.label: Server
items.desc: Replies to client requests and keeps no state.
